title: On the Ocean: the Massaliot, the Six Days North of Britain, and the Name That Was Taken
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Massalia, the Colony at the Mouth of the Rhone

stops.name: Massalia, the harbour of the Lacydon: a Greek born on a Gaulish shore
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: no ancient source gives a birth year, a father's name, or a death date; c. 350 BCE is inferred backward from the conventional date of the voyage
stops.campa: The Phocaeans built their town on the north shore of a rock inlet the Greeks call the Lacydon, and two and a half centuries later it is the richest Greek city on the Gaulish coast: a harbour where tin and amber arrive through Gaulish hands at Gaulish prices, because Carthage holds the western gate of the sea. Into this town Pytheas is born. The tradition preserves the city and nothing else. No father, no year, no house, no grave. He enters the record already grown, already a man who measures things.
suggested_refs: The harbour of the Lacydon, the modern Vieux-Port of Marseille, from which the voyage set out
sources: Strabo, Geography 4.1.4-5, on Massalia's wealth and trade

stops.name: Massalia, the gnomon at the summer solstice
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the measurement is attested only by its later reuse in Hipparchus and Eratosthenes and is never dated by any source; placed here before the voyage
stops.campa: He plants a shadow-stick in the ground and reads the noon of the longest day off it, and out of that ratio comes the latitude of Massalia. The figure is good. Hipparchus takes it up; Eratosthenes, building his map of the inhabited world at Alexandria, calibrates against it. Every other thing Pytheas will report gets called a lie by somebody. Nobody in antiquity disputes the shadow. Before he has seen the Ocean he has already done the work that makes his account usable to the men who refuse to believe the rest of it.
suggested_refs: The Massalia solstice shadow-ratio, reused by Hipparchus and Eratosthenes as a reference latitude
sources: Hipparchus, as reported in the later geographic tradition via Strabo

stops.name: Massalia, the setting out
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the voyage is dated only by cross-reference to Timaeus and Dicaearchus, who were near-contemporaries; no ancient source gives a year
stops.campa: He leaves for the Ocean. No fragment says on whose money, in what hull, or with how many men, and the silence will cost him his reputation: two centuries on, Polybius will ask how a private citizen of no fortune paid for such a journey and treat the unanswered question as proof the journey never happened. What Massalia wants is a route to tin and amber that does not run through other men's warehouses. What Pytheas brings back is that, and also a description of ice.
suggested_refs: The unanswered question of the voyage's funding, the hinge of Polybius's attack
sources: Barry Cunliffe, The Extraordinary Voyage of Pytheas the Greek (2001), not consulted directly

segments.name: Out of the Middle Sea and Up the Coast of Gaul

stops.name: The Pillars of Hercules: the passage nobody witnessed
stops.date_confidence: disputed: no surviving fragment states how Pytheas left the Mediterranean; Carthage controlled this strait, and an overland alternative is argued in the modern literature
stops.campa: Carthage holds both sides of the gate and bars Greek shipping through it. Whether Pytheas passed here at all is the first thing about him that cannot be settled: no line of any fragment says he did, and the whole southern route is a modern assumption resting on the fact that he was a sailor. The strait is where the argument against him begins. A man of no means, in a Greek hull, slipping past a Punic blockade, is either the most resourceful navigator of the century or a liar sitting at home in Massalia.
suggested_refs: The Carthaginian control of the Strait of Gibraltar in the late fourth century BCE

stops.name: Gadir, the temple of Melqart on the islet of Sancti Petri
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: no ancient source places Pytheas here, and the stop is inferred from standard periplus convention. The coordinate is corrected from a figure in circulation that falls twenty-two kilometres north, inside the Bay of Cadiz
stops.campa: On its islet at the edge of the Ocean stands the Phoenician sanctuary of Melqart, whom the Greeks call Herakles, the marker every periplus takes for the western end of the world. Strabo describes the Herakleion here. No source puts Pytheas on this shore. He is placed here by convention, because this is where ships out of the Middle Sea stop, and the honest statement is that the convention is doing all the work. From here the coast turns north and the sailing directions of the Greek world run out.
suggested_refs: The Melqart-Herakles sanctuary of Gades on the Sancti Petri islet
sources: Strabo, Geography 3.5.5, on the Herakleion at Gades
Inference from standard Phoenician and Greek periplus geography

stops.name: Burdigala on the Garonne: the road that avoids the sea
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: an alternative to the Gibraltar passage rather than a stop on the same route; associated with H. J. Mette's 1952 fragment edition and discussed in the modern literature
stops.campa: There is a second reconstruction, and it deletes the strait entirely. Massalia trades up the Rhone; from the Rhone a man crosses to the Garonne, and the Garonne runs down to the Gironde and the open Atlantic without passing a single Carthaginian hull. Scholars who take this route seriously make Pytheas a traveller who walked to the Ocean and took ship there. The two reconstructions cannot both be his. Neither is written down anywhere. The atlas keeps both pins and says which is which.
suggested_refs: H. J. Mette, Pytheas von Massalia (1952), the standard German fragment edition, not consulted directly
sources: Modern route reconstruction summarized in the secondary literature on Pytheas

stops.name: Corbilo on the Loire: the emporium quoted against him
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the site is archaeologically unlocated, the Loire having shifted its channels, and no fragment places Pytheas here. The common gloss calling Corbilo a great tin emporium appears in no ancient source
stops.campa: Strabo names Corbilo a former emporium on the Liger, and in the same breath repeats Polybius: that no Massaliot who spoke with Scipio could tell him one thing about Britain worth writing down. The passage is deployed as a weapon. If Pytheas's own countrymen knew nothing, then Pytheas knew nothing. The port has never been found; the river has moved. Later summaries turn Corbilo into a great tin market of the Gauls, which no ancient source says, and which this file does not repeat.
suggested_refs: The lost site of Corbilo on the Loire estuary
sources: Strabo, Geography 4.2.1, naming Corbilo and quoting Polybius on Scipio's Massaliot informants

stops.name: Pointe du Raz: the Ostimii at the end of Gaul
stops.date_confidence: attested claim, reconstructed placement: Strabo 1.4.5 quotes Pytheas on the Ostimii and the promontory Cabaeum; the identification with this headland is modern. Note that Pointe du Raz is in the Finistere department of Brittany and is not Cape Finisterre in Galicia
stops.campa: He names the Ostimii the westernmost people of Gaul, gives their promontory as Cabaeum, and sets the island Uxisame three days' sail out from it. Strabo copies the sentence down in order to break it: the distances, he says, are impossible. The fragment survives because a man who despised it needed the words in front of him to argue with. Every line of him that survives is a line somebody thought worth refuting. There is no other route out of antiquity.
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 1.4.5, on the Ostimii, Cabaeum, and Uxisame
sources: Strabo, Geography 1.4.5, trans. H. L. Jones (Loeb, 1917-32), via LacusCurtius

stops.name: Ushant, the island three days out
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: Uxisame is named in the fragment, the identification with Ushant is modern
stops.campa: Uxisame in the fragment, Ouessant on the chart: a low island in a race of tide off the Breton corner, where the coast of Gaul stops running north and the open crossing to Britain begins. Beyond this the Greek world has no sailing directions at all. Whatever Pytheas does next, he does without a periplus to follow, and the account he brings home will be the first one. It is also the point past which every fact he reports becomes, to Strabo and Polybius, a thing no honest man could have seen.
suggested_refs: Ouessant, ancient Uxisame, at the western corner of Brittany
sources: Modern route reconstruction, Cunliffe (2001), not consulted directly

segments.name: Britain: the Tin, the Circuit, the Tide

stops.name: Belerion, the tin-diggers of the western tip
stops.date_confidence: attested in Diodorus 5.21-22, but Diodorus names no source at that point; the chain running the passage back through Timaeus to Pytheas is modern inference
stops.campa: At the far western point the people are hospitable to strangers and civilised, the account says, by their traffic with foreign merchants. They work the tin-bearing ground, smelt the ore, and beat it into ingots shaped like knucklebones. It is the most concrete commercial passage anywhere in the tradition: not a marvel, not a monster, a description of an industry. Diodorus prints it without naming who saw it. Scholars run the line back through Timaeus to Pytheas, and are obliged to say so as an inference.
suggested_refs: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 5.21-22, on Belerion and the smelting of tin

stops.name: St Michael's Mount: the island called Ictis
stops.date_confidence: attested that Ictis existed, reconstructed as to which island it was; St Michael's Mount is one of two leading candidates and the identification has never been settled
stops.campa: The Britons drive the tin out on packhorses at low water to an island that becomes an island again when the tide comes back, and there the merchants buy it and carry it into Gaul. The tidal causeway is the detail that makes the passage read as seen rather than invented, and it is the reason this mount has been argued for since the eighteenth century. Ictis has never been identified. The pin is a candidate for a place that nobody, in two thousand years of looking, has been able to find.
suggested_refs: Diodorus Siculus 5.22, on the tin island of Ictis reachable on foot at low tide

stops.name: North Foreland: the promontory called Kantion
stops.date_confidence: attested: Kantion is named at Diodorus 5.21.3 and Strabo 1.4.3 attacks Pytheas's distance for it. Pliny NH 4.102, frequently cited here in secondary summaries, does not name Cantium at all
stops.campa: He fixes the south-eastern corner of Britain, and the fixing outlasts him: later geographers hang the outline of the whole island on this one named point. Strabo quotes the sentence and calls the distance absurd, several days' sail from Celtica to a headland a man can see across on a clear morning. The objection is fair and the number is wrong. The promontory is still there, and it still carries a version of the name a Massaliot gave it before Rome had a navy.
stops.quote: Pytheas declares that the length of Britain is more than twenty thousand stadia, and that Cantium is several days' sail from Celtica
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 1.4.3, trans. H. L. Jones (Loeb, 1917-32), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Diodorus Siculus 5.21.3, naming the promontory Kantion

stops.name: The Pentland Firth: a tide of a hundred and twenty feet
stops.date_confidence: attested figure, reconstructed placement: Pliny NH 2.99 locates the observation north of Britain without naming a strait. Note the correction, Pliny says north of Britain, not in Britain
stops.campa: North of Britain the water does something no Mediterranean sailor has a word for. Pliny records the figure Pytheas gave, a hundred and twenty Roman feet, eighty cubits in the older English renderings, and it is far too large; commentators ancient and modern call it exaggerated. It is also not made out of nothing. The races between the Orkneys and the mainland run at a speed that will stop a modern hull, and a man who had only ever seen the Mediterranean would reach for the largest number he owned.
stops.quote: Pytheas of Massilia states that north of Britain the tides rise 120 ft
stops.quote_source: Pliny, Natural History 2.99 (Loeb section 217), trans. H. Rackham (Loeb, 1938-63)
suggested_refs: Pliny, Natural History 2.99, on the tidal height reported by Pytheas

stops.name: Dunnet Head, the northern cape called Orcas
stops.date_confidence: attested that Pytheas gave a coastal circuit and that Diodorus names a northern promontory Orca; the circumnavigation rests on Strabo 2.4.1 reporting his claim to have travelled all of Britain that was accessible, which Strabo prints in order to deny it. Coordinate corrected eastward-drifting figures back onto the headland
stops.campa: The mainland ends. Diodorus calls the northern point Orca, and from a headland of this kind the open water begins. The circuit Pytheas gives for the island is more than forty thousand stadia; Diodorus prints forty-two thousand five hundred and names nobody; Pliny credits Pytheas and Isidorus jointly with four thousand eight hundred and seventy-five miles. Four numbers, three sources, no agreement between them. Every one is roughly the right order of magnitude for an island nobody had measured.
stops.quote: after asserting that he travelled over the whole of Britain that was accessible Pytheas reported that the coast-line of the island was more than forty thousand stadia
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 2.4.1, trans. H. L. Jones (Loeb, 1917-32), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: The four irreconcilable ancient figures for the circuit of Britain

stops.name: Ring of Brodgar, Orkney: the islands nobody attributed to him
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed and demoted: Pliny NH 4.103 lists forty Orcades but does not credit Pytheas, and Ptolemy, Mela and Tacitus name the group independently. The attribution of the island count to Pytheas, common in popular accounts, is unsupported
stops.campa: The stone ring on the Orkney mainland was already two thousand years old when a Greek sailed past it. Popular accounts credit Pytheas with the count of the Orcades, and the credit is not in the text: Pliny lists forty of them without saying who told him. What Pytheas is actually credited with is Orcas, the tip of the mainland, and the name sits close enough to the island group's that later readers slid one into the other. What survives of him here is a promontory name, and not one of the islands.
suggested_refs: Pliny, Natural History 4.103, listing forty Orcades without attribution
sources: Diodorus Siculus 5.21, on the promontory Orca

segments.name: Thule, and the Sea That Is Neither

stops.name: Unst, Shetland: the nearest Thule
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: one of several modern candidates for Thule. The coordinate is corrected to Skaw on the north-east tip of Unst, the northernmost settlement in the United Kingdom, rather than the island centroid used in some drafts
stops.campa: Six days' sail north of Britain, and Shetland is the nearest land that will fit a six-day figure if the wind is against him. Here at midsummer the light does not properly go: a twilight that lasts the night through, which the islanders call the simmer dim. It is not the true midnight sun, and that is the standing argument against Shetland. It would still have stopped a man from Massalia dead. He is further north than any Greek in the record, and Massalia has no vocabulary for a night like this.
suggested_refs: Skaw, Unst, the northernmost settlement in the United Kingdom, one candidate for Thule
sources: Modern identification debate summarized in Cunliffe (2001), not consulted directly

stops.name: Ultima Thule: six days' sail north of Britain
stops.date_confidence: disputed: the place is not identified and probably never will be. Candidates include Norway, Iceland, Shetland, the Faroes and Orkney. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical Thule pin, a Reykjavik proxy inherited byte-identical from columbus.journey.json and leif_erikson.journey.json, and it stands for an unlocated place
stops.campa: This is the pin the atlas already holds. Columbus comes here in February 1477 and writes that the sea was not frozen and the tides ran mightily; Leif Erikson's file carries the identical coordinate. Three travellers, one point, eighteen hundred years apart, and the two later ones are looking for the place the first one named. Pytheas gives it six days north of Britain and near the frozen sea, and that is the entire geographical content of the most famous name in the history of the north.
stops.quote: which Pytheas says is a six days' sail north of Britain, and is near the frozen sea
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 1.4.2, trans. H. L. Jones (Loeb, 1917-32), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: The canonical Thule pin shared with columbus.journey.json and leif_erikson.journey.json

stops.name: Trondheimsfjord: the second Thule
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: Norway is a leading modern candidate. The internal strain is recorded rather than repaired, since solstice-daylight arguments point at roughly 64 to 66 degrees north while Trondheim sits at 63.43. The frequent attribution of a Norway preference to Cunliffe could not be verified in any reachable source
stops.campa: The rival candidate is a coast, not an island. Norway lies at the latitude where the midsummer sun genuinely refuses to set, which Shetland does not, and if this is where he came then the frozen sea he reports lies further north again and he never touched it. The reasoning that brings scholars here is daylight arithmetic, and the arithmetic points a little further north than Trondheim itself does. Trondheim sits at 63.43 degrees north; the argument wants 64 to 66.
suggested_refs: The Norwegian candidacy for Thule, including the island of Smola
sources: Modern identification debate, Cunliffe (2001), not consulted directly

stops.name: The Arctic Circle on the Helgeland coast: where the barbarians show him the sun's bed
stops.date_confidence: attested fragment, symbolic placement: the coordinate marks the Arctic Circle where it crosses the Norwegian coast and is not a located site. Geminus's own floruit is disputed, c. 70 BCE on one reading of the Egyptian-calendar passage and as late as 50 CE on others
stops.campa: This is the closest the record comes to his own voice. The barbarians showed us. He does not present himself as discovering the short night; he presents himself as being taken to the place by people who live there and already know where the sun sleeps. Two hours for some, three for others, and then it comes back up. An astronomer copies the sentence out three centuries later without a word of ridicule, because to an astronomer it is what happens at that latitude.
stops.quote: And it seems that Pytheas of Massalia reached these places. At any rate, he says in his treatise On the Ocean that "the barbarians showed us where the Sun goes to sleep; for around these places it happens that the night becomes very short, 2 hours for some, 3 for others, so that, a little while after setting, the Sun rises straightaway."
stops.quote_source: Geminus, Introduction to the Phenomena VI 9, trans. J. Evans and J. L. Berggren, Geminos's Introduction to the Phenomena (Princeton, 2006)
suggested_refs: Geminus, Introduction to the Phenomena VI 9, the nearest surviving thing to Pytheas's own words
sources: Geminus, Introduction to the Phenomena VI 9, trans. Evans and Berggren (Princeton, 2006)

stops.name: Beyond Thule: the sea-lung
stops.date_confidence: attested fragment, symbolic placement: the coordinate marks the Greenland Sea pack-ice margin and is not a located site. Pliny 4.104 puts the frozen sea one day's sail beyond Thule, while Strabo 1.4.2 says only that Thule is near it; the two are not reconciled here
stops.campa: A day beyond, the sea stops being sea. Earth, water and air hold together in one suspension that can be neither sailed through nor walked on: a bond, he calls it, holding everything at once. Polybius quotes it as gibberish. Strabo quotes Polybius quoting it, as proof of fraud. Readers who have watched slush and grease ice forming on an autumn sea in the high north recognise the description at once. The most ridiculed sentence in the corpus is the one that reads most like an eyewitness.
stops.quote: a kind of substance concreted from all these elements, resembling a sea-lungs, a thing in which, he says, the earth, the sea, and all the elements are held in suspension
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 2.4.1, reporting Polybius reporting Pytheas, trans. H. L. Jones (Loeb, 1917-32), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: The sea-lung passage, Strabo 2.4.1, generally read as the earliest surviving description of pack ice

segments.name: The Amber Coast and the Return

stops.name: Skagen, the tip of Jutland: where the estuary may begin
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the localisation of Pytheas's northern estuary is entirely modern inference, and Jutland, per Humboldt, is one proposal among several. The ancient text fixes no position
stops.campa: Two seas meet at the point of Jutland and the water shows the seam. Somewhere on this coast, or six hundred miles east of it, or not here at all, lies the estuary the Loeb text calls Metuonis and the older reading calls Mentonomon. The ancient words fix nothing: an estuary of the Ocean, seven hundred and fifty miles long, a German people on its shores. Every pin on the amber coast is a guess wearing a Latin name, and the guesses run from Denmark to the mouth of the Vistula.
suggested_refs: The competing localisations of the Metuonis estuary: Jutland, Gotland, the Prussian Baltic coast, the Vistula mouth
sources: Modern reconstruction debate, Cunliffe (2001), not consulted directly

stops.name: The Sambia peninsula: amber burned for fuel
stops.date_confidence: attested fragment, reconstructed localisation: Pliny NH 37.35 gives the text verbatim, but the Sambian placement is modern inference and the ancient source fixes no location. The people are the Guiones or Gutones, not the Ostimii, who belong to the Breton fragment at the other end of the route
stops.campa: The Baltic throws amber onto its beaches in spring, and the people who gather it there burn it. They use it as fuel instead of wood, Pliny records, and sell it on to the Teutones next door. This is the far end of a trade that reaches Massalia priced like a jewel, and Pytheas has walked to the place where it washes up and is worth less than firewood. He also names the island it comes from Abalus. Timaeus, reading him, will rename the same island Basilia, and Pliny will contradict himself over which name is whose.
stops.quote: Pytheas speaks of an estuary of the Ocean named Metuonis and extending for 750 miles, the shores of which are inhabited by a German tribe, the Guiones. From here it is a day's sail to the Isle of Abalus, to which, he states, amber is carried in spring by currents, being an excretion consisting of solidified brine
stops.quote_source: Pliny, Natural History 37.35, trans. D. E. Eichholz (Loeb, 1962), via attalus.org
suggested_refs: Pliny NH 37.35-36 against Pliny NH 4.95: the Abalus and Basilia names, contradictory within one author
sources: Pliny, Natural History 37.35-36, trans. D. E. Eichholz (Loeb, 1962)

stops.name: Massalia, the return and the writing of On the Ocean
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the return is undated. The title is given as Peri tou Okeanou, On the Ocean, at Geminus VI 9; Periplus and Periodos Ges also circulate in the citation tradition
stops.campa: He comes home and writes it down: the tin island, the tidal causeway, the promontories, the eighty cubits of water, the two-hour night, the substance beyond Thule that is neither sea nor land. The book is called On the Ocean. It circulates for six hundred years, is quoted, argued with, plundered and mocked, and then goes out of the world entirely. Not one manuscript, not one papyrus scrap, not one line in his own hand. What survives is some thirty-nine fragments held in the mouths of men correcting him.
suggested_refs: Peri tou Okeanou, On the Ocean, lost by late antiquity; fragment editions Mette (1952) and Roseman (1994), neither consulted directly
sources: Geminus, Introduction to the Phenomena VI 9, naming the work

segments.name: The Book Survives in the Mouths of Its Enemies

stops.name: Athens, Timaeus in exile repeats him
stops.date_confidence: attested that Timaeus used Pytheas on the amber island; reconstructed that he is the channel for the Cornish tin and the circuit figure. Timaeus was exiled from Sicily by Agathocles c. 315-312 BCE and wrote his Histories over some fifty years in Athens, not in Sicily
stops.campa: Driven out of Sicily by Agathocles, Timaeus spends some fifty years in Athens writing a history of the west, and in it he takes up Pytheas. He repeats the amber island, giving it the name Basilia. He is probably the pipe through which the Cornish tin passage reaches Diodorus two centuries later. Probably: Diodorus names nobody at that point, and the Timaeus intermediary is a modern reconstruction argued from a preface. The first man to believe Pytheas is a man exiled from his own island.
suggested_refs: Walbank (1956), Mette (1952), Roller (2006) on the Timaeus intermediary, all known here only at second hand
sources: Timaeus, as cited by Pliny and Diodorus

stops.name: Alexandria, Eratosthenes uses the figures anyway
stops.date_confidence: attested via Strabo 1.4.2-4 and 2.5.8, reporting Eratosthenes's use of Pytheas's data; Eratosthenes's own text does not survive
stops.campa: The chief librarian is measuring the earth. To do it he needs latitudes, latitudes are scarce, and the Massaliot has supplied two: his own city's solstice shadow, and a northern figure for Thule. Eratosthenes takes them and builds them into the map. He is not being credulous; he is short of data. The most rigorous geographer of the age uses the numbers of the man later ages will call a fraud, because the numbers work and because nobody else has been where he says he has been.
suggested_refs: Eratosthenes's map of the inhabited world, calibrated in part on Pytheas's latitudes

stops.name: Rhodes, Hipparchus fixes the parallels
stops.date_confidence: attested via the later geographic tradition; Strabo preserves the substance of Hipparchus's use of Pytheas. Hipparchus was of Nicaea and observed at Rhodes
stops.campa: The astronomer who will give the West its star catalogue takes Pytheas's Massalia measurement and uses it to set a parallel of latitude, running the line east to Byzantium. He does not argue for it and he does not defend its author. Long after the tin and the amber and the frozen sea have been argued into disrepute, a shadow-length taken in a Gaulish harbour by a man nobody trusts is still sitting inside the mathematical framework of Greek geography, load-bearing and unremarked.
suggested_refs: The parallel of Massalia and Byzantium, set from Pytheas's solstice data
sources: Hipparchus, as reported through Strabo's geographic tradition

stops.name: Rome, Polybius asks who paid
stops.date_confidence: attested: preserved at Strabo 2.4.1, quoting Polybius. Polybius's own text of the passage does not survive independently
stops.campa: The attack that sticks is not geographical. Polybius does not go to Britain and check; he asks a question about money. A private man, and a poor one, does not fund an expedition of that length, therefore the expedition did not happen, therefore the book is invention. It is an argument from plausibility, made by a historian who prided himself on going and looking, and it works, because no fragment anywhere says who paid. Two thousand years later nobody can answer it either.
stops.quote: it is incredible that a private individual, and a poor man too, could have travelled such distances by sea and by land
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 2.4.1, quoting Polybius, trans. H. L. Jones (Loeb, 1917-32), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Polybius's funding objection, the most durable ancient argument against the voyage

stops.name: Rhodes, Geminus copies out the sentence without laughing
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed date and place: Geminus's floruit is disputed, c. 70 BCE on one reading and as late as 50 CE on others, and 'of Rhodes' is an inference from references to Rhodian mountains rather than an attested epithet
stops.campa: An astronomer writing an elementary handbook needs an example of what happens to the night as a traveller goes north, so he reaches for On the Ocean and quotes it, naming the book and the man. No polemic, no sneer, and no defence either. To Geminus the two-hour night is not a traveller's tale requiring belief; it is a consequence of the obliquity of the ecliptic, and Pytheas simply happens to be the person who went and saw it. The witness who takes no side is the one who understood the claim.
suggested_refs: Geminus, Introduction to the Phenomena, book VI, on the length of the night at northern latitudes
sources: Geminus, Introduction to the Phenomena VI 9

stops.name: Agyrium, Diodorus carries the tin and the amber into a universal history
stops.date_confidence: attested that Diodorus 5.21-22 carries the material; reconstructed that Pytheas is its ultimate source, since Diodorus names no authority at that point and never mentions Timaeus there
stops.campa: In Book Five the Sicilian sets down Belerion and its hospitable tin-workers, the island reachable at low water, the northern promontory Orca, and the circuit of Britain at forty-two thousand five hundred stadia. He credits none of it to anybody. Every modern reader who wants to call this Pytheas has to route it through Timaeus first, and say so out loud. The richest surviving description of Britain before Caesar enters the record with no author's name attached to it.
suggested_refs: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica, Book 5, the unattributed British material

stops.name: Amaseia, Strabo names him an arch-falsifier
stops.date_confidence: attested: the charge is verbatim at Strabo 1.4.3. Note that Strabo probably never saw the original book and worked from intermediaries, and that the common claim that he preserves the most fragments is contested against Pliny
stops.campa: Strabo calls him an arch-falsifier and returns to him again and again, book after book, quoting in order to demolish. And in the middle of the demolition he transcribes the one sentence that shows Pytheas grading his own evidence: the sea-lung he saw himself, the rest he had from other men. A liar does not label his hearsay. The prosecutor enters into the record, without noticing, the exhibit that most damages his own case, and then goes on to the next charge.
stops.quote: Now, as for this thing that resembles the sea-lungs, he says that he saw it himself, but that all the rest he tells from hearsay
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 2.4.1, trans. H. L. Jones (Loeb, 1917-32), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 1.4.3, the arch-falsifier verdict, verified verbatim
sources: Strabo, Geography 1.4.3 and 2.4.1, trans. H. L. Jones (Loeb, 1917-32), via LacusCurtius

stops.name: Rome, Pliny the Elder copies him down
stops.date_confidence: attested: Pliny cites Pytheas across books 2, 4 and 37 and does not resolve the contradictions between Pytheas and Timaeus that he himself records
stops.campa: The compiler of the Naturalis Historia works the way he always works, out of earlier books rather than out of his own eyes, and for once the method saves something. He takes Pytheas on the tides, on Thule, on the circuit of Britain, on the amber and the island of Abalus, and prints him as a source rather than a scandal. He also contradicts himself between Book Four and Book Thirty-seven about which island name belongs to whom, and lets the contradiction stand.
stops.quote: Its circumference is reported by Pytheas and Isidorus to measure 4875 miles
stops.quote_source: Pliny, Natural History 4.102, trans. H. Rackham (Loeb, 1938-63), via attalus.org
suggested_refs: Pliny, Natural History books 2, 4 and 37, the fullest surviving body of near-verbatim Pytheas

segments.name: Ultima Thule: the Name Outlives the Report

stops.name: Rome, Virgil sets Thule at the edge of the world
stops.date_confidence: attested: Virgil, Georgics 1.30
stops.campa: In the first book of the Georgics, flattering a young Caesar with the offer of the whole earth, Virgil reaches for the furthest thing he can name and writes ultima Thule. Two words. They detach from the poem immediately, and from Pytheas entirely. From here on Thule is not a place six days north of Britain with a two-hour night; it is a figure of speech meaning the limit, available to anyone, requiring no evidence and admitting no correction. The poet does more for the name than the navigator ever did.
suggested_refs: Virgil, Georgics 1.30, the coining of ultima Thule

stops.name: Constantinople, Procopius puts thirteen tribes on Thule
stops.date_confidence: attested: Procopius, De Bello Gothico. The identification of his Thule with Scandinavia is the standard modern reading
stops.campa: Writing the Gothic War, Procopius describes Thule as a great northern island holding thirteen tribes with kings over them, and what he is describing is plainly Scandinavia. Eight hundred years after the fragment, the name has slid off whatever Pytheas found and fastened onto a landmass he may never have reached. Nobody notices the substitution. Thule now means wherever the north is currently thought to end, and it will keep moving for another thousand years.
suggested_refs: Procopius, De Bello Gothico, on Thule and its thirteen tribes

stops.name: Seville, Isidore fixes Thule in the Etymologies
stops.date_confidence: attested: Isidore of Seville, Etymologiae 14.6.4. The composition date is conventional
stops.campa: The bishop compiling the encyclopaedia that will teach the Latin Middle Ages what the world contains gives Thule an entry: the last island of the ocean, in the north. No caveat, no source-criticism, no six days' sail, no frozen sea, no Massaliot. The geography survives and the evidence behind it is stripped out at the door. Every medieval reader who meets the word meets it in this form, as a fact of the world rather than as one man's disputed report of a voyage.
suggested_refs: Isidore of Seville, Etymologiae 14.6.4, the Thule entry

stops.name: Iceland, the monks Dicuil questioned
stops.date_confidence: attested: Dicuil, De mensura orbis terrae, reporting clerics who claimed to have been there. The identification of their island with Iceland is standard but is not stated by Dicuil. Coordinate inherited from the atlas's canonical Thule pin
stops.campa: An Irish monk in Francia writes down what other monks told him: that they had sailed to an island in the north where at midsummer the sun did not set, and a man could pick the lice out of his shirt at midnight as easily as at noon. Eleven hundred and fifty years after the fragment, ordinary clerics report the two-hour night as something they saw. Nobody calls them arch-falsifiers. Columbus will reach this same coordinate in 1477, and Leif Erikson's file already shares it.
suggested_refs: Dicuil, De mensura orbis terrae, on the clerics who saw the midnight sun

stops.name: Knebworth House, the study: Vril
stops.date_confidence: attested: The Coming Race published anonymously by Blackwood in May 1871. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from bulwer_lytton.journey.json
stops.campa: In his study at Knebworth, Edward Bulwer-Lytton writes The Coming Race and invents a word for a force that heals and destroys: vril. He tells John Forster he means electricity, developed to uses only dimly guessed at. The word leaves the novel and never returns to it. Nothing in this room touches Pytheas. But the vril of the next fifty years will need a homeland to have come from, and the only spare homeland in the European imagination is the one a Greek reported and a Roman poet turned into a phrase.
suggested_refs: The Coming Race (1871), Blackwood, published anonymously

stops.name: London, Lansdowne Road: Blavatsky makes Vril a fact of nature
stops.date_confidence: attested: The Secret Doctrine published 20 October 1888. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from blavatsky.journey.json
stops.campa: From the house in Holland Park, Helena Blavatsky publishes The Secret Doctrine and folds Bulwer-Lytton's invented force into a cosmology of root-races, taking vril for a fact of nature rather than a device of fiction. The root-races need geographies: a drowned Atlantis, a polar Hyperborea. Hyperborea is older than Pytheas and he never used the word. It is about to be welded to his Thule so thoroughly that the two will not come apart again, and her shadow-heirs will do the welding.
suggested_refs: H. P. Blavatsky, The Secret Doctrine (1888), the root-race cosmology
sources: Strabo, Geography, on the ancient conflation of Thule with Hyperborean legend

stops.name: Munich, the Thule Society takes the name
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Thule-Gesellschaft was dedicated under that name in Munich on 18 August 1918 under Sebottendorff. Reconstructed as to venue: the Hotel Vier Jahreszeiten is documented as headquarters and meeting rooms rather than as an attested founding site. Coordinate inherited from maria_orsic.journey.json
stops.campa: Rudolf von Sebottendorff's lodge of runes and Germanic myth takes for itself the name of an island a Massaliot navigator reported as lying six days north of Britain, near a frozen sea. In the lodge it means the lost homeland of an Aryan race. There is no bridge between the two meanings. There is only a word emptied out by twenty-two centuries of poetry and encyclopaedias until anything at all could be poured into it, and this is what gets poured. Theodor Reuss retires into this same ecology in 1921.
suggested_refs: The Thule-Gesellschaft, dedicated Munich, 18 August 1918
Reginald Phelps, 'Before Hitler Came' (1963)

stops.name: Munich, the Vril Gesellschaft takes the word
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the earliest hard trace of the society is a recollection written down in 1947. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from bulwer_lytton.journey.json
stops.campa: A street away from the Thule lodge, Maria Orsic and her circle name themselves out of an English novel. Vril from Knebworth, Thule from Massalia, Hyperborea from Blavatsky by way of Pindar: three unrelated words from three unrelated centuries, assembled into one mythology in one Bavarian city in a single year. Savitri Devi will later supply the Hyperborean descent that binds them together. None of them could have read Pytheas, whose book had been gone from the world for fifteen hundred years.
suggested_refs: Willy Ley's 1947 recollection, the earliest hard trace of the Vril circle

stops.name: Iceland, the Ahnenerbe goes looking for Thule
stops.date_confidence: attested and corrected: the Ahnenerbe was founded by Himmler on 1 July 1935 and sent no expeditions that year. Three expeditions went to Iceland in 1938, explicitly seeking Thule as birthplace of the Aryan race. Accounts dating expeditions to 1935 are wrong on both halves
stops.campa: Himmler's research bureau sends men to Iceland to find the birthplace of a race. They go to Bohuslan and Karelia, to Val Camonica, to Tibet, and three times in one year to this island, hunting physical evidence for a homeland that exists because a Greek merchant said he sailed six days north of Britain and a Roman poet put two words in a poem. It is the coordinate Columbus recorded in 1477 and Dicuil's monks described in the ninth century. The expeditions find nothing, which was the only available result.
suggested_refs: The three Ahnenerbe expeditions to Iceland, 1938
sources: Documented history of the Ahnenerbe's expeditions under Himmler

stops.name: Greenwich Island, Serrano reads the ice as Hyperborea
stops.date_confidence: traditional: coordinate inherited byte-identical from serrano.journey.json
stops.campa: At the far end of the other axis of the earth, Miguel Serrano walks the black shore of Base Soberania in a light that never wholly dies, and begins reading Antarctica as a text of Atlantis and Hyperborea. He will write it out later as El Cordon Dorado: Hyperborea and the Black Sun, the destruction of the polar homeland. The frozen sea Pytheas described has travelled from one pole to the other and hardened into a doctrine. Nothing of the fragments is left in it except the ice, and the light that will not go out.
suggested_refs: Miguel Serrano, El Cordon Dorado: Hitlerismo Esoterico
Base Soberania, Greenwich Island, South Shetlands

stops.name: Marseille, the Palais de la Bourse: the city puts him on the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested that Auguste Ottin (1811-1890) sculpted the Pytheas figure on the facade of the Palais de la Bourse, paired with the Massaliot explorer Euthymenes; the exact year within the building programme is not fixed here
stops.campa: Auguste Ottin carves him into the front of the merchants' exchange, paired with Euthymenes, the other Massaliot who sailed out of the known sea. Twenty-two centuries after Polybius asked how a poor man could have paid for such a voyage, the chamber of commerce of Marseille answers the question by claiming him as its own. He has no grave anywhere in the world, and not even a lost-tomb legend to trace. This wall, a few streets from the Lacydon, is the nearest thing he has.
suggested_refs: Auguste Ottin's Pytheas on the Palais de la Bourse facade, Marseille, paired with Euthymenes
sources: Public monument, Palais de la Bourse facade sculpture programme, Marseille

stops.name: Oxford, the fragments reassembled
stops.date_confidence: attested: Barry Cunliffe, The Extraordinary Voyage of Pytheas the Greek, Walker and Co, New York, 2001; Penguin issued the UK edition in 2002. Cunliffe's specific Thule identification could not be verified in any reachable source and is not asserted here
stops.campa: A professor of European archaeology gathers every surviving fragment and puts a route back together, and the modern verdict inverts the ancient one: not a fabulist but an observer, doing real astronomy from a hull at the edge of what a Greek could reach. The reconstruction is a best guess and remains one. Not one line of the book itself has ever been found, in any library or any papyrus, and the two standard fragment editions, Mette and Roseman, both open by admitting how little there is.
suggested_refs: Barry Cunliffe, The Extraordinary Voyage of Pytheas the Greek (Walker and Co, 2001)
H. J. Mette (1952) and C. H. Roseman (1994), the standard fragment editions
sources: Barry Cunliffe, The Extraordinary Voyage of Pytheas the Greek (2001), not consulted directly

stops.name: Laurel, Maryland: Ultima Thule is given back its name
stops.date_confidence: attested and corrected: NASA chose the nickname Ultima Thule on 13 March 2018 after a public campaign, the New Horizons flyby was 1 January 2019, and the IAU announced the permanent name Arrokoth in November 2019, with the ceremony at NASA Headquarters on 12 November and the permission of Pamunkey elders of the Powhatan nation. The coordinate is the Applied Physics Laboratory, the mission's operations centre, standing in for a body in the Kuiper Belt that has no terrestrial position
stops.campa: A spacecraft passes a two-lobed rock four billion miles out, and for twenty months the rock is called Ultima Thule, because the phrase still means the furthest thing there is. Then the name is given up. Munich got there first, and what Sebottendorff's lodge did to the word cannot be undone by good intentions. The object is renamed Arrokoth, sky, in the language of the Powhatan, with the permission of Pamunkey elders. Pytheas reported an island. Everything after that was done to the name by other people.
suggested_refs: The IAU naming of Arrokoth, announced November 2019, ceremony at NASA Headquarters 12 November 2019
sources: NASA New Horizons mission naming announcements
